title: The barber paradox
hook: A barber who shaves only those who do not shave themselves cannot exist.
peek: A village barber shaves everyone who does not shave themselves, and nobody else. Does he shave himself? Either answer breaks the rule. The puzzle is a friendly version of Russell's paradox, which in 1901 shook the foundations of mathematics.
lede: Picture a village where the barber shaves all those, and only those, who do not shave themselves. Does the barber shave himself? If he does, he breaks his rule. If he does not, the rule says he must. The answer is that no such barber can exist. Bertrand Russell used the story to explain a far more serious problem he had found in logic.

bullets.text: In 1901 Russell considered the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. Is that set a member of itself? Like the barber, it is if and only if it is not, which showed that collecting things freely into sets leads to contradiction.

In 1902 Russell wrote to Gottlob Frege, whose second volume on the logical foundations of arithmetic was going to press. Frege saw that the paradox undermined his system and added an appendix admitting the problem.

bullets.opening: A paradox or just a riddle
bullets.text: Russell himself said the barber is not a perfect match. The barber story simply proves a certain barber is impossible, while the set version struck at ideas mathematicians had relied on.

Fixes followed. Russell developed a theory of types, used in Principia Mathematica, and Ernst Zermelo proposed rules in 1908 for which sets may exist. Refined, those rules underpin most of modern mathematics.
